summary:
Desarrollamos un sistema de monitoreo de salud para astronautas en misiones de larga duración, como un viaje a Marte. El sistema tiene tres partes que trabajan juntas:
1.Un traje con sensores textiles que mide corazón, respiración, oxígeno, temperatura, movimiento, estrés, sueño, posibles enfermedades y radiación.
2.Un software de monitoreo con una silueta humana interactiva, con una vista para el astronauta y otra para el Control en Tierra.
3.Ivy, una asistente de inteligencia artificial con voz que vigila los datos, conversa con el astronauta y actúa cuando hace falta: avisa al astronauta, al compañero y a Tierra.
Ivy es una herramienta de apoyo a la decisión y evaluación de riesgo. No sustituye a un médico ni emite diagnósticos definitivos.
details:
Ivy: medical assistant and health monitoring for astronauts

Phoenix MIR Team · November 14, 2026

Team members: (fill in the team names)

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Ivy is a health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions, such as a trip to Mars. It has three parts that work together:

•     A suit with textile sensors that measures heart, breathing, oxygen, temperature, movement, stress, sleep and radiation.

•     Monitoring software (dashboard) with an interactive human silhouette. Each body zone changes color (green, yellow or red) and, when clicked, shows its chart and trend. It has one view for the astronaut and a more detailed one for Ground Control.

•     Ivy, a voice-enabled artificial intelligence assistant that watches the data, talks with the astronaut and acts when needed.

Data flow: suit sensors → central module (ESP32-S3) → Bluetooth → hub (Raspberry Pi) → Ivy → dashboard, earpiece and alerts.

Ivy works in three ways:

•     Real-time emergencies. Fixed rules compare each measurement against safety ranges. A critical condition must repeat in two consecutive readings, and if a sensor is loose or the arm is moving a lot, Ivy only asks the astronaut to check the sensor. If the emergency is real, Ivy alerts the astronaut, the crewmate and Earth, and asks “Are you okay?”. If the astronaut does not answer within 8 seconds, Ivy escalates to the crewmate for possible loss of consciousness.

•     Long-term risks. Each astronaut’s first 5 days define their personal baseline. After that, Ivy tracks daily trends (resting heart rate, HRV, nighttime temperature, exercise, radiation dose) to detect slow changes the astronaut would not notice, such as infection, anemia, or bone and muscle loss.

•     Conversation and companionship. Ivy only responds when it hears its name. Critical alerts are the exception: they play on their own, because an unconscious astronaut cannot call Ivy. Ivy also runs a daily voice check-in (dizziness, tiredness, mood, vision and a reflex test) and measures how long the astronaut has gone without human contact to help with isolation.

Ivy is a decision-support and risk-assessment tool. It does not replace a doctor and does not give definitive diagnoses.

2. What benefits does it offer?

•     Early detection: finds changes over days or weeks that the astronaut would not notice on their own.

•     Immediate emergency response: alerts all three parties (astronaut, crewmate and Earth) and escalates if there is no answer.

•     Personalized assessment: compares against each person’s own baseline, not only general values.

•     Fewer false alarms: checks signal quality, discards readings taken during movement and asks for confirmation with repeated readings.

•     Mental health support: daily check-in, isolation mode and an alert to the psychologist on Earth when needed.

•     Clear information: a color-coded silhouette the astronaut understands at a glance, with more detail for Ground Control.

•     Works offline and protects privacy: voice is processed locally, no audio is stored, and slow-risk medical data is not shared with the crewmate.

3. What is the expected impact of the project?

On distant missions, astronauts are largely responsible for detecting changes in their own bodies. Space exposes them to radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment, and this affects the whole body. Ivy is designed to cover those effects:

System

Effect of space and what Ivy monitors

Blood

Fewer red and white blood cells (anemia, more infections). Measured hemoglobin and indirect signals.

Radiation

Cataracts, DNA damage, higher cancer risk. Dose rate, accumulated dose and a solar storm alert with an order to go to the shelter.

Brain

Dizziness and loss of orientation. Daily voice check-in and reflex test.

Heart and vessels

Vessels that age faster and insulin resistance. ECG, HRV, arterial stiffness and glucose.

Muscles and bones

Loss of mass, strength and bone density (up to 1.5% per month). Exercise, strength and daily mechanical load.

 

With this, the project aims to make a long mission depend less on communication with Earth, which has delays and outages, and to give the medical team on Earth organized data and alerts with a confidence level so they can decide better.

Current status: it is a prototype that works with simulated data. The thresholds are example values and must be validated with flight surgeons. The next steps are to connect the real hardware and voice, and to test the system with volunteers in a simulated confinement.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware or software were used?

Area

Tools

Central module

XIAO ESP32-S3, AD8232 amplifier and LiPo battery, in a 3D-printed TPU case

Suit sensors

Conductive fabric electrodes with silver thread (ECG), conductive rubber band (breathing), MAX30205 or TMP117 (temperature), MAX30102 (pulse and SpO₂), GSR sensor (sweat), MPU6050 IMU (movement and exercise) and SBM-20 Geiger-Müller tube (radiation)

Voice

Bone-conduction earpiece with a microphone

Hub

Raspberry Pi, connected to the central module over Bluetooth

Software languages

Python 3, standard library only (assistant and long-term risks), and HTML, CSS and JavaScript (dashboard), developed in Visual Studio Code with Live Server

Communication

HTTP connection between the dashboard and Ivy (read status, send alerts and show notices on screen)

Artificial intelligence

Language model that works with context (reference protocols, normal ranges and astronaut data), not trained from scratch. The Claude API is used for the demo, and a local model is planned

Voice (to be connected)

Wake-word detector for “Ivy” (openWakeWord or Porcupine), speech-to-text (Whisper or Vosk) and text-to-speech (Piper or Coqui)

Proposed improvements

Thigh EMG (MyoWare), insoles with force sensors and an IMU on the headband

 

5. In what way is the project creative?

•     A companion, not just a data panel. Ivy has a name and a voice, talks with the astronaut and keeps them company throughout the mission.

•     Fixed rules plus AI. Critical alerts are generated by deterministic rules, not by the AI model, so an emergency is never missed because of a model error. The AI is used to converse, explain and guide.

•     Care against isolation. Ivy measures time without human contact and does not count talking to itself, because it does not want to replace people. It suggests activities (video call, eating with the crewmate, looking at Earth) and alerts the psychologist if needed.

•     Health tailored to each person. The personal baseline makes it possible to detect a change even when the value still looks normal in general.

•     We expanded the challenge. We reviewed the effects of space on the body and added what was missing: arterial stiffness, hemoglobin and glucose, a voice check for dizziness and reflexes, and mechanical load on the bones.

•     A textile, detachable suit, with conductive thread and a removable module so it can be washed.

•     Interactive silhouette with a color traffic light and two views, one for the astronaut and one for Earth.

•     Demonstration without hardware or real radiation: data and solar storms are simulated by software.

6. What factors did the team take into account?

•     Real effects of space on the body: blood, radiation, brain, heart, muscles and bones, and what the suit cannot measure (covered with periodic manual tests).

•     Safety: critical rules take priority over the AI, false positives are avoided and, if the connection with the sensors is lost, Ivy says so instead of staying silent.

•     Limited communication: on a real mission there are delays and outages, so the system must work locally on the spacecraft.

•     Mental health: isolation, mood and sleep. Whether isolation notices are spoken or only shown on screen is still to be defined with the mission psychologist.

•     Privacy and ethics: voice is processed locally and no audio is stored. Ivy gives risk assessments with a confidence level, not diagnoses, and any medical decision belongs to a doctor. All alerts are kept in an audit log.

•     Astronaut comfort: Ivy only responds when it hears its name, does not speak while the astronaut sleeps and keeps low-priority notices on screen only.

•     Honesty about limitations: the thresholds are examples, arterial stiffness is an experimental indicator, bone loss is a risk index and not a measurement, the dosimeter only measures natural radiation and the prototype has not been validated with people.
